analysis.one_liner: Caps pay for executives of banks bailed out with taxpayer rescue funds at the President's salary.
analysis.headline: The bill had 45 House sponsors but never got a committee vote; it died in the House Financial Services Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2008 financial crisis, the government gave banks and other companies rescue money through the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP). This bill said that any officer, director, or employee of a company taking that money could not be paid more than the President of the United States, counting salary, bonuses, stock options, retirement benefits, and every other form of pay. The limit would last as long as the company still owed the government, and the Treasury Secretary would have to claw back pay already granted above the cap.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who funded the bank bailouts. Executive pay at rescued firms would come out of companies propped up with public money, so capping it keeps bailout dollars from flowing out as multimillion-dollar compensation packages while the public is still owed money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers who funded the bank rescues

how_it_helps.text: Bars any employee of a TARP-funded company from receiving annual compensation above what the President is paid, counting wages, bonuses, deferred pay, retirement contributions, stock options, property, and anything else the Treasury Secretary counts as compensation.
Applies not only to new rescue money but to any modification of assistance already received, and stays in force for as long as the company still has assistance or obligations outstanding under TARP.
Directs the Treasury Secretary to write rules to carry out the limit, including reimbursing compensation amounts already paid above the cap, so the limit has enforcement teeth.

analysis.who_pays: Executives and directors of banks and other companies that received or modified TARP assistance. Their total pay, including bonuses and options, would be capped at the presidential salary for as long as their company remained on public assistance. Companies could escape the cap only by fully exiting TARP.

drawbacks.text: The cap covered only companies still holding TARP assistance, so banks that repaid their rescue funds would be exempt, and compensation at the rest of the financial industry would be untouched. By the time of introduction, many large TARP recipients were already moving to repay.

A hard cap tied to the presidency is a blunt tool: it could push top talent out of the very firms taxpayers had a stake in rescuing, and give companies an incentive to restructure pay into forms the Treasury Secretary might not classify as compensation, an outcome the bill tries to head off by leaving the definition of compensation largely to the Secretary's discretion.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core logic is straightforward: money funneled to failing banks through a $700 billion rescue program should not be paying out as executive bonuses while the public is on the hook. The cost is concentrated on a few hundred executives at rescued firms, and the risk of driving away leadership at fragile companies is real but modest, since firms could always repay TARP to regain freedom on pay. The bill's main weakness is its narrowness: it reaches only TARP recipients and leaves the broader executive-pay practices that fueled the crisis unregulated.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Dennis Moore of Kansas introduced the Limit Executive Compensation Abuse Act on February 4, 2009, with 44 Democratic cosponsors joining him, amid the debate over pay at companies rescued through TARP.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day it was introduced.
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action ever occurred; the bill stayed in committee until the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives and directors of TARP-assisted financial institutions, whose pay was never capped by this bill. The House leadership and the Financial Services Committee were also spared a politically charged vote on banker pay during the bailout era.

for.name: Dennis Moore
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill the day it was introduced and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Barney Frank
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for consideration or a markup.

sides.party_line_note: All 45 sponsors were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never left a committee controlled by the Democratic majority.

industries.industry: Executives and directors of TARP-assisted financial institutions
industries.note: The bill would cap their total annual pay at the presidential salary for as long as their firms held public rescue funds, including clawing back amounts already paid above the cap. Their gain under the status quo came at the direct expense of taxpayers funding the rescue.

industries.industry: TARP recipient banks and financial firms
industries.note: The limit attached to receiving assistance, so firms could avoid it by fully repaying TARP, but while on assistance their ability to attract and retain executives with large pay packages would be constrained. Firms had an interest in keeping the bill off the floor.
